rows.12:10cc:
...So, it's finally my turn to speak.
My name is Shoji Arai.
I'm a second-year.
Tell me, do you all like movies?
I love them.
French films in particular.
European cinema is wonderful, isn't it?
The images are beautiful and poetic; they cleanse the soul.
What about you, {a}?{p}Do you like French films?
rows.12:1224:
...What a pitiful person you are.
To think you've never yet encountered such splendor.
You really must see one.
I'm sure you'll come to love them.
...Could it be, {a}, that you dislike movies in general?
rows.12:12f4:
Oh, is that so?
You like movies, and yet you don't watch French films.
What an odd person you are.
But then, everyone is different.{p}
rows.12:1410: So, what genre of movies do you like?
rows.12:1498:
Heh heh... So you like sci-fi and horror?
You have rather vulgar taste, don't you?{p}
rows.12:14f4:
I don't much care for that type of film myself.
Above all, they have no class.
The story is just tacked on as an afterthought, and far too many of them rely on nothing but scares for the eye and special effects.
...But movies are frightening, aren't they?
No, I don't mean horror movies.
I mean film itself.
Don't you think so?
People have long said that photographs steal a person's soul, haven't they?
Nowadays we laugh that off as superstition, but back then people seriously believed it.
That every photo taken of you shortened your life, or that when three people are photographed together, the one in the middle dies young.
Back then, I suppose photography must have seemed utterly uncanny.
Your own image, sealed inside a single sheet of paper.
It truly was magic.
And so everyone feared it.
It's the same with movies.
When movies were first born, they caused quite a stir.
For example, a character in a film fires a gun right at the screen, you see?
They say the audience watching it fainted, thinking they'd been shot dead.
People even believed that different people lived beyond that silver screen, and that they were watching the world those people lived in.
Nowadays no one believes that, of course.
...But is it really a lie?
Was what people believed back then truly just their imagination?
I can't quite bring myself to think so.
Sometimes film captures things that should never be filmed, or strange things that don't exist in reality...
I can't shake the feeling that film has that kind of uncanny power.
What I'm about to tell you is the story of one such movie.{p}
rows.12:1ae8:
There was a boy in my class named Yasuo Tokita.
He loved movies like no one else, and he often talked to me about them.
And my, did he know a lot.
A real film fanatic, I suppose you'd call him.
I thought I knew quite a lot myself, but there's always someone better.
He had me beat.
There was hardly a movie he hadn't seen.
Even when I did desperate research, trying to show him up, it was no use.
There's the expression "walking encyclopedia," and when it came to movies, that's exactly what he was.
Being such a movie lover, Tokita deeply regretted that our school had no film club of any kind.
After all, his dream, of course, was to become a film director.
So he went and started one himself.
Back then, we were first-years.{p}
rows.12:1d88:
Even so, Tokita actively reached out to upperclassmen and teachers, and in no time at all he'd founded a film society.
Naturally, it couldn't become an official club right away.
It turns out there are quite a lot of movie lovers, if you look for them.
All told, about twenty people joined, I heard.
He was overjoyed.{p}
rows.12:1eac:
He brought most of the filming equipment himself.
Though by equipment, I just mean an 8mm camera and some simple lighting gear.
And by 8mm, I don't mean the kind of video camera everyone uses now.
I mean an old-fashioned handheld 8mm film camera.
You don't see many of those these days.
Even so, the members were thrilled, I hear.
After all, they got to play at making a real movie.
They felt a bit like professionals.{p}
rows.12:2038:
Hm?
Me?
Did I join that Film Research Society, you ask?
No, I didn't.
I was in the soccer club, you see.
Is it funny, me being in the soccer club?
Well, that's a story for another time.
By the way, what about you?{p}Would you be interested in a film research society?
rows.12:2148:
I see.
So you're interested.
Then if it were you, what job would you want to take on?
There are so many jobs in filmmaking, after all.{p}
rows.12:2204:
Oh, you're quite the connoisseur.
Well, whether a movie turns out good or bad is decided almost entirely by the director.{p}
rows.12:2270:
But it seems most people say actor.
Actors stand out, after all; it's flashy and glamorous.
And the actors are the ones who become popular.
If you screened your own movie at the school festival, whoever played the lead would become a star.
Provided the movie was any good, of course.
Starstruck types watch movies for the actors.
But connoisseurs watch them for the director.
Naturally, Tokita wanted to direct.
Well, I suppose most of the people who joined were the starstruck type.{p}
rows.12:24fc:
And so filming began on the society's memorable first production.
I think it was right around this time last year.
...You like horror and sci-fi movies, didn't you say?
As it happens, so did he.
The movie he set out to make was a horror film titled 'The Mummy Man and the Beauty.'
Now, don't laugh at the title.
What he wanted to make wasn't one of today's SFX films loaded with special effects; if anything, he wanted to make an old-fashioned monster movie from the golden age.
Not that he could have pulled off flashy special effects even if he'd tried.
So instead of fussing over that sort of thing, he poured himself into dark direction and atmosphere, so that even a cheap monster in a simple costume and makeup would look real.{p}
rows.12:27a8:
He worked truly hard at it.
People who are eager at first gradually lose interest; that's how it goes.
In the end, they only do what they want to, and won't touch anything that bores them or takes real work.
Most of them had joined half for fun, after all.
Even so, Tokita kept at it, helped by the very few who shared his ambition, handling everything from odd jobs to acting.
In my heart, I was cheering him on.
What was the movie about?
Tokita wrote the script too.
The basic plot goes like this.{p}
rows.12:297c:
A mummy brought over from Egypt comes back to life and searches for the reincarnation of the princess it once served.
In the end, it turns her into a mummy too, places her in its own coffin with it, and the two of them return to Egypt together.
Simple, isn't it?
Well, the actors were all hams.
And they were students, too.
Most of it is set in the school.
So the heroine is a student at this school, too, wearing a sailor uniform.
And she's supposed to be the reincarnation of an Egyptian princess.
Rather a dubious premise, isn't it?
Even so, somehow or other, they finished filming.{p}
rows.12:2b88:
But that's when the hard part begins.
You probably think that once you've shot it, the movie is done, but you'd be dead wrong.
Whether it turns out interesting or not depends entirely on the editing that comes next.
You take all the scattered scenes captured on the film you've shot and splice them together, one by one.
And then a single movie is complete.
Apparently, it's work that takes a great deal of patience.
Though for someone who loves it, I suppose it's irresistibly fun.
And Tokita was one of those people.
He threw himself into the editing, losing all track of time.{p}
rows.12:2d88:
"...Huh?
That's weird.
Did I shoot a scene like this?"
Looking at one of the reels, he tilted his head, puzzled.
It was a scene with the Mummy Man.
The scene where the Mummy Man lumbers around in the dark, searching for the reincarnated princess.
He had indeed shot a similar scene, but this one matched neither his memory nor his storyboards.
When you make a movie, you first draw up what's called a storyboard.
Then you shoot each scene to match it.
Otherwise, by the time you finish shooting, you can't make heads or tails of anything, and you can't shoot efficiently in the limited time you have.{p}
rows.12:3078:
The film clearly showed the mummy's face.
And it was far more grotesque and realistic than the makeup he had applied.
Even Tokita, who must have seen countless horror movies, felt a chill run down his spine when he saw that film.
That's how well it was shot.
He had no memory of shooting a cut like that.
But maybe he was misremembering.
There was no way Tokita wouldn't use a scene that good.
He edited it in.{p}
rows.12:3254:
But the next day, while looking at some other film, he found yet another scene he didn't remember shooting.
When you shoot a movie, you run many times more film than the actual running time.
So you end up with a huge number of reels.
This was the scene where a detective investigating a mysterious string of murders is killed by the Mummy Man.{p}
rows.12:3398:
Of course, the detective was played by one of the film society members.
The actual death scene was a simple one.
The detective, attacked by the mummy, runs away.
The mummy's hands reach for the detective's neck, and the screen goes black.
Then comes the detective's scream.{p}
rows.12:3480: After that, a close-up of the mummy's bloodied hands.{p}
rows.12:34b8:
Yet that film clearly showed the detective dying.
And how realistic it was!
The detective barely had any screen time.
You see, the boy who played him was such a terrible actor that they couldn't give him much screen time.
And yet here was an utterly convincing performance.
The detective being strangled by the mummy, his face twisted in agony.
Then a single thread of bright red blood spilling from the corner of his mouth.
The detective collapsing to the ground and going still.
One cut after another like that appeared on the screen.{p}
rows.12:3750: It was the very next day.
rows.12:3774: The student who played the detective was killed.
rows.12:37c4:
When Tokita heard how it happened, he couldn't believe his ears.
It was exactly like that scene, wasn't it?
Apparently, no one knows who strangled him.
After all, he had been asleep alone in his own room in the middle of the night.
There was no sign that anyone had snuck in, and the room hadn't been disturbed.
So naturally, suspicion falls on the family.
Tokita grew terrified.
What if he had died because Tokita had watched that film...
What if this was the mummy's curse...
What would you think, in his place?
Would you want to keep editing that movie?{p}If you did, something even stranger might show up on the film.
rows.12:3a3c:
Heh heh... How cruel you are.
With a personality like that, I won't be responsible for what becomes of you.
But Tokita was the same.
He loved movies to death, after all.
This movie might become a masterpiece for the ages.
When he thought that, he wanted to keep editing more than anything.{p}
rows.12:3b48: And sure enough, the film he watched that day had something even stranger on it.
rows.12:3b9c:
This time, it was the scene where the heroine, the reincarnated princess, is shut inside the coffin.
In the script, she sees the mummy, faints from sheer terror, and is then shut inside the mummy's coffin.{p}
rows.12:3c60:
But what do you know?
What that film showed was a scene of cruelty so savage you'd want to look away.{p}
rows.12:3ce0:
The mummy crushed her in its arms so hard that her insides burst.
And then, of all things, it began tearing off her arms and legs.
One by one, carefully.
She wasn't dead yet.
She twisted her bloodied body, thrashing desperately to get away from the mummy.
But it was no use.
Once the mummy had torn off every last one of her limbs, it tossed them into the coffin.
Then, at last, it twisted off her head and carelessly threw the rest of her body into the coffin.
And then it rubbed its cheek against her head and hugged it close.{p}
rows.12:3ec0:
And with that, the film ended.
Tokita stared at the scene, stunned.
There are all sorts of horror movies, and the ones with one bloody scene after another are called splatter films, or gore flicks.
But the images now burned into Tokita's mind were beyond anything such feeble terms could describe.
"...I've never seen a movie like this."
It's strange, considering he was supposedly the one filming it.
The movie had taken on a life of its own.
That's what Tokita thought, and he watched the scene over and over again.
No matter how many times he watched it, it never lost its freshness.{p}
rows.12:416c:
Naturally, he used that scene for the movie's climax.
Of course, there was no way a movie with such extreme gore spliced into it could be screened at school.
Even so, he was satisfied.
He was convinced that, as an independent film, it would succeed wherever he pitched it.{p}
rows.12:426c: It was the very next day.{p}
rows.12:4290:
...I'm sure you've guessed by now.
The girl who played the heroine was found brutally murdered.
They say her body was in pieces.
Of course, I never heard the details, but Tokita knew.
What state the body was in, and how she was killed.
And that the proof was all recorded on that reel.
It was after school that very day, as I recall.
That Tokita came up to me and told me how realistic and amazing this movie was.{p}
rows.12:4458:
"I'm making an amazing movie right now.
It's a masterpiece, no doubt about it.
It's going to go down in history.
...You like movies, don't you?
If you want, I could show you a little of what I'm editing."
That's how I came to hear about this movie.
I gladly tagged along after him.
I was so excited.
...Well?
If you got an invitation like that, would you have high hopes for the movie?{p}Or would you sneer at it, figuring it's just some amateur production anyway?
rows.12:4618: Can't tell until I see it

notes: 12:24fc: 'You like horror and sci-fi movies, didn't you say?' is fixed text regardless of the earlier genre choice, as in the source.
